additionalTime: 1 hour dough chill, at least 2 hours shaped-crust chill, 15 minutes par-baked-crust cooling, and at least 4 hours final cooling
author: Robert Carr
description: A deep-dish blueberry pie with a vivid fresh-and-wild blueberry lemon filling, a flaky egg-white-sealed butter crust, and a crisp brown butter lemon-oat crumble with caramelized clusters.
equipment: 4 to 5 cups granulated sugar or at least 2 pounds ceramic pie weights, for blind baking

ingredients: 1 2/3 cups (200 grams) moderate-protein all-purpose flour, for the crust
1 tablespoon (12 grams) granulated sugar, for the crust
1 teaspoon (3 grams) Diamond Crystal kosher salt, for the crust
10 tablespoons (142 grams) unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes and chilled until firm but pliable, for the crust
1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar
4 to 5 tablespoons (60 to 75 grams) ice water
Up to 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour, for rolling the crust
1 large egg white, lightly beaten, for sealing the crust
24 ounces (680 grams) fresh cultivated blueberries, rinsed only if needed and dried completely
8 ounces (225 grams) frozen wild blueberries, kept frozen
5 teaspoons finely grated lemon zest, divided, from about 3 large lemons
3 tablespoons (45 grams) fresh lemon juice
1 cup plus 2 tablespoons (225 grams) granulated sugar, for the filling
46 grams cassava-based tapioca starch
1/2 teaspoon (2 grams) Diamond Crystal kosher salt, for the filling
1/4 teaspoon ground coriander
8 tablespoons (113 grams) unsalted butter, for the crumble
1 tablespoon (15 grams) room-temperature water, for the crumble
1 cup (120 grams) all-purpose flour, for the crumble
1/2 cup (45 grams) old-fashioned rolled oats
1/3 cup packed (71 grams) light brown sugar
2 tablespoons (25 grams) granulated sugar, for the crumble
1/2 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt, for the crumble
instructions: Make the crust dough: in a medium bowl, whisk together 1 2/3 cups (200 grams) moderate-protein all-purpose flour, 1 tablespoon (12 grams) granulated sugar, and 1 teaspoon (3 grams) Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

Add 10 tablespoons (142 grams) chilled butter cubes and toss until every piece is coated with flour. Working quickly, flatten each cube once between your fingertips into a thin shard about 1/4 inch thick. Stop while the butter remains visibly distinct; do not work it down to uniformly pea-size crumbs.

Combine 1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar with 4 tablespoons (60 grams) ice water. Drizzle it evenly over the flour-butter mixture while tossing with a fork or flexible spatula. Squeeze a handful of dough; if it holds together without crumbling, stop. If dry flour remains, add the final 1 tablespoon (15 grams) ice water 1 teaspoon at a time.

Turn the shaggy dough onto a clean surface and press it into a rough rectangle. Fold it into thirds like a letter, rotate it 90 degrees, and gently press it into a 1-inch-thick disk. Wrap tightly and refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to 24 hours.

Make the crumble while the dough chills: melt 8 tablespoons (113 grams) unsalted butter in a light-colored medium saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring and scraping the bottom often, until the sputtering subsides and the milk solids turn deep golden brown and smell nutty, about 5 to 7 minutes after the butter melts. Do not let the solids turn black.

Immediately pour the brown butter, including all browned bits, into a medium heatproof bowl. Cool for 10 minutes, then slowly stir in 1 tablespoon (15 grams) room-temperature water to replace moisture lost during browning.

Combine 1/3 cup packed (71 grams) light brown sugar, 2 tablespoons (25 grams) granulated sugar, and 2 teaspoons of the lemon zest in a small bowl. Rub the zest into the sugars with your fingertips until the mixture feels slightly damp and smells strongly of lemon.

Stir the lemon-infused sugars, 1 cup (120 grams) all-purpose flour, 1/2 cup (45 grams) old-fashioned rolled oats, and 1/2 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt into the brown butter until no dry flour remains. Compress about two-thirds of the mixture into irregular 1/2-inch clumps and leave the rest as smaller crumbs. Cover and refrigerate until firm, at least 30 minutes.

Remove the chilled crust dough from the refrigerator. If it is too firm to roll without cracking, let it stand at room temperature for 5 to 10 minutes. The dough should feel cool and pliable, never greasy or sticky.

Dust the work surface and rolling pin with enough of the reserved flour to prevent sticking. Roll the dough from the center outward into a 14-inch round, rotating it frequently. Brush away loose excess flour before transferring the dough.

Gently settle the dough into a 9-inch deep-dish metal pie pan without stretching it. Press it against the bottom and sides, trim the overhang to 1 inch, tuck the overhang under itself, and crimp the edge. Cover without pressing on the crimp and refrigerate for at least 2 hours and up to 24 hours so the gluten can relax and the butter can become thoroughly firm.
Place a baking steel or pizza stone on the lower-middle oven rack with a rimmed aluminum baking sheet on top. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F for at least 45 minutes.

Line the thoroughly chilled crust with a large sheet of heavy-duty aluminum foil, pressing it flush against the bottom, sides, and crimp. Fill the shell completely to the rim with granulated sugar reserved for use as a reusable pie weight, or with enough ceramic pie weights to support the sides fully.

Place the pie pan on the hot rimmed baking sheet and bake for 25 minutes, until the edge is set and only faintly colored. Carefully lift out the foil and weights. Cool the sugar completely before storing it for future baking.

Immediately brush the bottom and sides of the hot crust with a thin, even layer of the lightly beaten egg white, avoiding puddles. Return the crust to the hot baking sheet and bake for 5 to 7 minutes, until the coating looks dry and the bottom is just beginning to color. Transfer the crust to a wire rack and cool for 15 minutes. Increase the oven temperature to 400 degrees F.

Make the filling while the crust cools: combine 1 cup plus 2 tablespoons (225 grams) granulated sugar and the remaining 1 tablespoon lemon zest in a large mixing bowl. Rub the zest into the sugar until it feels damp and highly fragrant.
Whisk in 46 grams cassava-based tapioca starch, 1/2 teaspoon (2 grams) Diamond Crystal kosher salt, and 1/4 teaspoon ground coriander until evenly distributed with no visible starch clumps.

Add 24 ounces (680 grams) completely dry fresh cultivated blueberries, 8 ounces (225 grams) frozen wild blueberries, and 3 tablespoons (45 grams) fresh lemon juice. Fold gently with a flexible spatula until every berry is evenly coated. Let the filling stand for 15 minutes, then fold once more from the bottom to redistribute the juices and starch.
Scrape the filling and every drop of accumulated juice into the par-baked crust. Spread the berries into an even layer without crushing them.

Break the chilled crumble into a mixture of 1/4- to 3/4-inch clusters and smaller crumbs. Scatter it evenly over the filling, covering most of the berries while leaving several narrow gaps where steam can escape.
Bake the assembled pie on the hot rimmed baking sheet at 400 degrees F for 20 minutes.

Reduce the oven temperature to 375 degrees F and continue baking for 45 to 60 minutes. The pie is done when the crumble is deeply golden and the filling produces slow, thick bubbles in several places within 2 inches of the center, not only around the edge. A thermometer inserted through an exposed gap into the center of the filling should register about 212 to 213 degrees F at low elevation.

Shield the crimped edge with foil if it becomes deeply browned. If the crumble reaches a deep golden brown before the filling bubbles near the center, loosely tent the entire pie with foil and continue baking until the filling is fully cooked.
Transfer the pie to a wire rack and cool completely, uncovered, for at least 4 hours and preferably until the center is no warmer than 85 degrees F. Do not cover or slice the pie while it is warm.
notes: Use the gram measurements whenever possible. The filling is calibrated to 905 grams of fruit, and small changes to the sugar or tapioca starch can noticeably change the final set.
Use a moderate-protein all-purpose flour for the crust rather than bread flour or a particularly high-protein all-purpose flour. Excess protein can make the crust tougher and more prone to shrinking.
Keep visible, flattened shards of butter in the crust dough. Those distinct layers create a flakier crust than reducing all of the butter to uniformly small crumbs.
The shaped crust must rest in the refrigerator for at least 2 hours. The initial dough chill alone does not replace this rest because rolling and crimping warm and stress the dough again.
Heavy-duty foil conforms to the crust more closely than parchment. Fill the lined shell completely to the rim so the bottom and sloped sides are supported during the par-bake.
Granulated sugar is the preferred pie weight because it is heavy and settles into the shape of the shell. It is not consumed by the recipe and can be cooled, stored, and reused.
The egg white coating and partial blind bake protect the bottom crust from the raw berry filling without fully baking the shell before the long fruit-pie bake.
Rinse the fresh blueberries only if needed, and dry them completely. Water clinging to the fruit changes the filling ratio and can soften the final set.
Do not thaw the frozen wild blueberries. They provide a deeper, more concentrated blueberry flavor while the cultivated berries provide larger, juicier fruit.
Use cassava-based tapioca starch rather than quick-cooking tapioca pearls. Do not substitute the same quantity of cornstarch, flour, or Instant ClearJel because each thickener behaves differently.

The filling uses 225 grams of sugar and 46 grams of cassava tapioca starch, closely scaling the proven blueberry-pie ratio to 905 grams of fruit. Do not reduce the filling sugar independently; it affects both flavor and the way the tapioca sets during the long bake.
The filling is intentionally not precooked. Baking the berries from raw preserves their natural juice and fresher blueberry flavor instead of turning part of the filling into a reduced jam.
The coriander should not be identifiable as a spice. At 1/4 teaspoon, it reinforces the floral and citrus-like aromas already present in blueberries.

The crumble uses both brown and granulated sugar: brown sugar contributes caramel depth, while granulated sugar produces a cleaner, crisper finish. Cinnamon, vanilla, nuts, and almond extract are intentionally omitted so blueberry, lemon, brown butter, and toasted oats remain the dominant flavors.
Adding 1 tablespoon water to the brown butter replaces moisture lost during browning and helps the crumble form crisp, irregular clusters rather than becoming greasy or sandy.
The pie is not done when only the outer filling bubbles. Wait for slow, thick bubbling near the center so the tapioca starch is fully activated.
Cooling to 85 degrees F or below is essential for clean slices. The filling will remain loose if the pie is cut while warm.
For the crispest crust and crumble, serve the pie the day it is baked. Store leftovers loosely covered at room temperature for up to 2 days or refrigerated for up to 4 days.
To refresh refrigerated slices, warm them on a baking sheet in a 350 degrees F oven for 8 to 10 minutes, then let them stand for 10 minutes before serving.
personalNotes: The pie was good. It took a long time to make. The pie crust was a bit of a pain to make and after the pie was finished, it seemed like all the flattened tablespoons of butter in the crust were hard to cut through. The pie crust was still good, but I think it could be better. Before cooking the berry mix was so good, after cooking it seemed to lose a bit of that flavor. Note to myself, instructions for making the pie crust need to be more clear, as well as when rolling it out.
title: Blueberry Lemon Crumble Pie
